summary: Gives interworking guidelines between the widely used but nonstandard SIP Diversion header and the standard History-Info header, for conveying call diversion information. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 7544.

plainLanguage.summary: Two different notes say a phone call was forwarded. This explains how to translate between them. It has been replaced by RFC 7544.

questions: how to map diversion to history-info
what is the sip diversion header
subtitle: How to translate call-forwarding history between SIP's widely deployed Diversion header and the standard History-Info header.

tldr.problem: Many SIP networks record call forwarding in the non-standard Diversion header, while the IETF standard is the History-Info header. Mixing them carelessly can leave the two inconsistent.
tldr.mechanism: A border device converts entries one way or the other using mapping tables for reason codes, order, counters and privacy, and avoids leaving both headers independently in the same INVITE.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational, Independent Submission meant to ease migration to History-Info. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7544.

facts.label: Entries created
facts.value: N Diversion entries become N+1 History-Info entries

today: RFC 6044 is an Informational Independent Submission that has been obsoleted by RFC 7544. The Diversion header it deals with is documented as Historic in RFC 5806, and the standard History-Info header is defined in RFC 4244.

sections.title: Two Headers for Call Diversion
sections.content:
Services such as voicemail, interactive voice recognition and automatic call distribution work better when the called SIP user agent can tell from whom and why a session was diverted. SIP can carry that information in two headers: the standard History-Info header (RFC 4244) and the Diversion header, which is documented as Historic in RFC 5806.

Diversion is not standardized but is widely used, because most existing implementations adopted it when no standard solution was ready. The RFC says new implementation and deployment of Diversion is strongly discouraged. The goal is to let the two interwork and so help migration from non-standard deployments toward the IETF specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Some phones leave a note saying 'this call was forwarded' in an old style, and newer ones use an official style. This guide helps the two styles understand each other.

sections.title: Scope and Coexistence Policy
sections.content:
The interworking is normally done by a SIP border device that knows by configuration that it sits between a region using History-Info and one using Diversion. Diversion and History-Info MUST NOT independently coexist in the same session signaling, because the diversion information could become mixed up or inconsistent.

The mapping works only where History-Info carries the diversion reason in a cause URI parameter. That use is specific to the 3GPP Communication Diversion specification, so implementations that do not use cause for call forwarding are not covered.

Going from Diversion to History-Info, the Diversion header should be removed from the outgoing INVITE, since all its information is carried over. If a History-Info header is already present, only diversion information not yet in it is added as the last (most recent) entry. Going the other way, History-Info that holds only call-forwarding data is deleted after conversion, but if it holds other information it is kept as received and forwarded, and only the diverting-user information is used to build Diversion entries.

History-Info is chronological, with the oldest entry first. Diversion is in reverse chronology, so its first entry is the last diverting user.
sections.plainLanguage: You should never leave two different forwarding notes on the same call, because they might disagree. One note is turned into the other, and the old one is thrown away, unless it holds other useful facts.

sections.title: The Two Header Formats
sections.content:
A History-Info entry is a targeted-to URI followed by parameters, including an index of digits separated by dots (for example 1.1.1) that records the forward hops and retargets. A diverting reason can be expressed with the cause URI parameter from RFC 4458, whose value is a SIP status code. The presence of cause shows that the entry is a diverting user; the diverting user is located in the entry before the one containing the cause value. A Privacy header with the value history may be included in an entry.

A Diversion entry is a name-addr followed by optional parameters: reason (such as unknown, user-busy, no-answer, unavailable, unconditional, time-of-day, do-not-disturb, deflection, follow-me, out-of-service or away), counter, limit, privacy and screen.
sections.plainLanguage: One note lists the forwards from oldest to newest and gives each a number. The other lists them newest first and writes a reason such as 'busy' or 'no answer' beside each.

sections.title: Mapping Diversion to History-Info
sections.content:
For N Diversion entries, N+1 History-Info entries are created. Diversion entries are mapped from the bottom-most to the top-most so the new entries appear in the order the diversions occurred. The first entry takes the bottom-most Diversion address and index=1. Each following entry increments the previous index with .1 and takes a cause value from the previous Diversion entry's reason. A last entry is created from the Request-URI of the INVITE, with the cause from the top-most Diversion entry.

Reasons without a close equivalent map to a default of 404. A privacy value of full, name or uri maps to history, and off maps to an absent or none Privacy header.

A Diversion counter greater than 1 means several successive redirections. History-Info has no counter, so the converter creates N-1 placeholder entries, such as <sip:unknown@unknown.invalid;cause=xxx>, so the number of diversions stays visible. A tel: URI cannot be used in History-Info, so a SIP URI with user=phone is suggested. Other optional Diversion parameters have no recommended mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: To go from the old note to the new one, you copy each forward in the order it happened, give it a number, and translate the reason into a code. If the old note said 'forwarded three times', you add blank stand-ins so the count still shows.

sections.title: Mapping History-Info to Diversion
sections.content:
In the other direction, History-Info entries are mapped from the top-most to the bottom-most, so the first selected entry becomes the last Diversion entry. One Diversion entry is created for each entry that precedes a cause parameter, with the address of that preceding entry as its name-addr. The cause code gives the reason: 302 to unconditional, 486 to user-busy, 408 to no-answer, 480 or 487 to deflection, 503 to unavailable, and 404 to unknown. The counter is set to 1, and a Privacy of history becomes full, while absent or none becomes off.

The mapping applies only to INVITE requests. In 3xx responses both headers may appear, and a proxy that wants to interwork should apply the mapping there. Where History-Info entries come from sequential forking (an incremented index), the converter may create only a Diversion entry or skip the mapping, according to local policy. The same logic applies to the Voicemail URI case in the appendix.
sections.plainLanguage: Going back, you read the new note from oldest to newest, turn each reason code back into a plain word like 'busy', and write them out newest-first as the old note expects.

sections.title: Privacy and Integrity
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4244 and RFC 5806 apply. Both headers must respect the privacy and integrity each diverting user asks for. Without integrity, requested privacy could be downgraded or removed, exposing identity information. Without confidentiality, eavesdroppers could read personal information that the user asked a privacy service to hide.

Unauthorized insertion, deletion or modification of these headers can mislead users and applications. A SIP entity that can give a redirection reason in either header should be able to suppress it in line with the privacy requirements of the user concerned.
sections.plainLanguage: Forwarding notes can reveal who called whom, so they must stay private and must not be tampered with on the way.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE FROM SECTION 7.1: DIVERSION MAPPED INTO HISTORY-INFO

data.title: Diversion changed into History-Info
data.code:
Diversion:
diverting_user3_address;reason=unconditional;counter=1;privacy=off,
diverting_user2_address;reason=user-busy;counter=1;privacy=full,
diverting_user1_address;reason=no-answer;counter=1;privacy=off

Mapped into:

History-Info:
<sip: diverting_user1_address; privacy=none >; index=1,
<sip: diverting_user2_address; cause=408?privacy=history>;index=1.1,
<sip: diverting_user3_address; cause=486?privacy=none>;index=1.1.1,
<sip: last_diverting_target; cause=302>;index=1.1.1.1
